The African Founder of the Future:

In wealthier economies, a founder can hire their way out of most weaknesses. A CFO handles the money, a consultant handles the rules, an agency handles the brand. Across much of Africa those specialists are thin on the ground, so the founder does that work personally.

Economists call this an institutional void. Some systems businesses lean on elsewhere, credit bureaus, expert recruiters, contract enforcement, are still forming here. A founder who understands this learns to supply that support themselves.

That means the founder of the future needs real fluency in nine areas:
Finance. Raising and structuring money when local funding is scarce and currencies move against you.

Technology. Understanding it well enough to make good decisions, not just hiring someone and walking away.

Leadership. Coaching your team yourself, since strong management training is still rare here.
Global markets. The African Continental Free Trade Area puts 1.3 billion people within reach now, not someday.

Brand. Where trust systems are still forming, your brand is the proof people rely on before they buy from you.

Operations. Delivering consistently despite unreliable power and logistics is a real advantage.
Policy. Rules can change overnight and reshape a market, so watching policy is part of the job.

People. Skilled workers keep leaving for opportunities abroad, so keeping good people takes constant work.

Strategy. The judgment that ties all of this together and decides what you handle yourself.

Grit gets a founder through the first year. This decides if they are still standing a decade later.
Which of these are you handling alone that a more developed market would have handled for you?

I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.
 
"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"
 
I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
 
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.
 
That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:

Send request → check status code → check response body

What seniors answer:

Contract validation across consumers
Schema drift detection
State injection to remove UI dependency
Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail
 
The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
 
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.
 
It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.
 
What was your "I didn't know what I didn't know" API testing moment?

The "Qualified but Unhired" Paradox:

 Why Life Science Graduates Struggle to Enter Pharma, despite meeting all academic criteria, thousands of fresh life science graduates face automated rejection emails when applying for entry-level pharmaceutical roles. 
This systemic hiring paradox stems from four core bottlenecks: a stringent industry requirement for prior experience, a gap between theoretical university coursework and strict compliance frameworks (like GMP, GLP, and QA/QC), an accelerating digital shift toward AI and bioinformatics, and a hyper-saturated applicant pool holding identical, unspecialized degrees.
To bridge this gap and stand out, candidates must actively transition from being merely "eligible" to genuinely "industry-ready":

 * Target High-Demand Niches: Pursue short certifications in Regulatory Affairs, Pharmacovigilance, or Clinical Data Management rather than applying only to generic lab roles.

 * Leverage Gateway Avenues: Target Contract Research Organizations (CROs), CDMOs, or QA/QC roles, which frequently hire fresh talent and provide crucial regulated experience.

 * Reframe Resume Language: Translate academic lab work into industry value by highlighting standard operating procedures (SOPs), compliance standards, and analytical documentation.

 * Build Digital & Regulatory Skills: Gain foundational literacy in data analytics tools (like Python, SQL, or R) and familiarize yourself with global regulatory standards (FDA, EMA).

 * Network Beyond Job Portals: Reach out to university alumni in target companies and engage publicly with industry news to build professional visibility.

The pharma industry isn't short on open roles—it is looking for candidates who understand how science operates inside a regulated commercial environment.

Every HTTP status code is a test case waiting to be written.
Most QA engineers check for 200 and move on.

That's how the worst API bug ships: a 200 response with an empty body.
The status code isn't the result. It's the instruction for what to test next.

A few that catch people:
201 Created - don't trust it. GET the resource back and confirm it exists.
204 No Content assert the body IS empty. A 204 with a payload is a contract break.

401 vs 403 - 401 is "who are you?", 403 is "I know you, you still can't." Test both with the same endpoint.
409 Conflict - fire two creates at once. If you never see a 409, your concurrency handling is fake.
422 - valid JSON, broken business rule. The case most teams skip entirely.
429 - if you can't trigger a rate limit, you can't prove one exists.

504 - slow the upstream. Watch whether your retry logic wakes up or melts down.

The full map is in the image. Save it.
Junior testers verify the happy path. Senior testers know every code is a door to a failure mode.

Sometimes, the hardest part of an interview is not the interview itself.
It’s what happens after it.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been actively interviewing.

In 10+ companies, I’ve reached different stages: L2, L3, technical discussions, managerial rounds, and even final-stage conversations.

Some interviews went really well.
Some discussions lasted more than an hour.
In a few, I came out genuinely thinking, “This could be the one.”
And then comes the waiting.
One day.
Three days.
A week.
You check your phone when a notification comes in.
You open LinkedIn a little more often.
You wonder whether you should follow up again or just wait.
Sometimes there is a response.
Sometimes there isn’t.
I understand the other side too.
Hiring teams may be waiting for approvals.
Budgets can change.
Roles can be put on hold.
There may be other candidates in the process.

But as a candidate, after spending hours preparing for multiple rounds, understanding the company and product, rearranging your schedule, and giving your best in every conversation, silence is probably the hardest feedback to process.

This phase has taught me something important:
Never stop your journey while waiting for one result.
Keep applying.
Keep having conversations.
Keep preparing.
Keep improving.

Because until there is a written offer, an interview is still an opportunity, not an outcome.

At the same time, even a small message like:

“We are still evaluating your profile. We’ll get back to you shortly.”

can mean a lot to someone waiting on the other side.

I’m still continuing my journey and currently exploring remote, full-time, contract, freelance, project-based, and senior Backend / AI Engineering opportunities.

The last few weeks have had a lot of waiting, but they’ve also given me stronger technical conversations, better clarity, and a better understanding of what I’m looking for next.
To everyone currently going through interview rounds and waiting for that one message:
Keep going. One pending response should never stop the next opportunity.

I’d genuinely love to know:
Have you ever reached L2, L3, or the final stage of an interview and then heard nothing for days? How did you handle it?

Why the Right Hiring Partner Makes All the Difference

In today’s competitive hiring environment, finding candidates is not the only challenge.

The real challenge is finding the right candidate, at the right time, with the right fit — and getting them to join.

For many businesses, a vacancy that remains open for weeks can affect productivity, project timelines, customer commitments and, ultimately, revenue.

This is where the right hiring partner can make a meaningful difference.
Hiring is not just about filling positions

A recruitment partner should do more than forward CVs.
Effective hiring requires understanding:

What the business actually needs
Which skills are essential for the role
Whether the candidate is genuinely interested
Their availability and notice period
Compensation expectations
Cultural and role fit
Whether the candidate is likely to stay long term
A large database of candidates does not automatically translate into successful hiring.
Quality matters more than quantity.
The importance of joining timelines

One of the biggest challenges businesses face today is the gap between selecting a candidate and actually getting them onboarded.
A candidate may be excellent on paper but have a 60–90 day notice period.
When a business needs someone urgently, that timeline may simply not work.
At SAM Manpower & Career Services LLP, we focus strongly on candidates who can join within 0–30 days, helping organisations address hiring requirements where waiting for long notice periods isn't practical.
What a good hiring partner should bring to the table
1. Access to relevant talent
Businesses need relevant profiles, not hundreds of random CVs.
A focused recruitment process helps reduce the time hiring teams spend screening unsuitable candidates.
2. Faster hiring cycles
When positions are business-critical, speed matters.
A recruitment partner with an understanding of immediate and short-notice joiners can help organisations move from requirement to onboarding faster.
3. Flexible workforce solutions
Hiring requirements are not always the same.
Depending on the business situation, organisations may need:
Permanent Recruitment | IT Contract Staffing | Payroll Outsourcing | Workforce Management | HRMS Solutions
Having access to multiple workforce solutions allows businesses to choose an approach that fits their actual requirement.
4. Technology-assisted hiring
Recruitment is becoming increasingly technology-driven.
AI-based CV screening, structured assessments and HR technology can help recruiters improve efficiency while allowing them to spend more time on what technology cannot replace — understanding people and business requirements.
5. A long-term approach
The objective should not simply be to close today's vacancy.
A good hiring relationship should help a business build a dependable talent pipeline and reduce repeated hiring challenges over time.

BEFORE YOU HIRE AN AI DEVELOPMENT COMPANY, ASK THIS.

You’ve seen the demo.
The AI looks impressive.
The proposal promises a fast launch.

But before you sign the contract, ask yourself:
“Do I really know what I’m buying?”

Choosing the wrong AI development partner can mean months of delays, unexpected costs, security risks, and a product that never makes it into production.

Before signing, make sure your potential partner can clearly answer:
- What business outcome will AI improve?
Not “AI transformation.” Ask for a specific metric—revenue, retention, support cost, conversion, or productivity.

- Who owns my data, code and AI assets?
Your contract should clearly cover source code, models, prompts, datasets, infrastructure and IP.

- How will you prove the AI actually works?
Ask about evaluation datasets, accuracy thresholds, testing and human review—not just a demo.

- What happens when the AI gets it wrong?
Production AI needs fallback mechanisms, confidence thresholds, human escalation and monitoring.

- How will it integrate with my existing systems?
CRM, ERP, databases, APIs and authentication often become the real development challenge.

- Who is actually building my product?
Meet the engineers. Understand their experience, roles and availability—not just the sales team.

- How will my data stay secure?
Ask where data is processed, who can access it, how it is stored, and what compliance standards are followed.

- What happens after launch?
AI isn't “build once and forget.” Models, prompts, data and user behavior change continuously.

Upwork Isn't Dying. It's Firing Its Smallest Clients. Here's What That Means For You.

I read something last week that changed how I look at Upwork.
An analyst wrote: "Upwork isn't losing clients. It's firing them."
And the data backs it up.

Here's what's actually happening:
Active clients have dropped for 8 consecutive quarters. From 868,000 in Q2 2024 to 763,000 in Q2 2026.

Sounds like a dying marketplace, right?

Wrong.

Because spending per client hit a record $5,230 - up 5% year-over-year, and it's risen for 8 straight quarters.

The clients who are leaving? They're the small, low-complexity, low-ticket customers. The ones who used to post $50 jobs. The ones AI is eating.
The clients who are staying? They're spending more. On bigger, more complex projects.

What does this mean for you?
Upwork is becoming a high-value, AI-driven platform. And the freelancers who win will be the ones who adapt.

But there's a problem.
Problem 1: Most freelancers are still competing for work that's disappearing.
Short, repeatable, low-complexity tasks? AI is automating them. Upwork's own CEO said AI "degraded the volume of client activity on the low end, impacting contracts of $500 and below".

Problem 2: Ghost jobs are draining Connects.
Clients face zero penalties for letting a job post die. Freelancers spend Connects, get nothing, and no refunds are issued.
One 13-year veteran with $100K+ earned said: "I saw a 102 Connects bid for a single job. This is no longer a marketplace. It's a gambling den."

Problem 3: Uma AI decides who gets seen.
In May 2026, Upwork eliminated Specialized Profiles. Now, Uma - Upwork's AI - decides which freelancers get highlighted "for every client and every opportunity".

If your profile is vague or generic, Uma can't categorize you. And if Uma can't categorize you, clients never see you.

So what do you actually do?

Three things that work right now:
1. Stop being a generalist.
"Web Developer | Designer | SEO Expert" confuses the AI. Pick one niche. Get specific. Clarity beats talent when the gatekeeper is an algorithm.

2. Treat every Connect like it's your last.
Check the client's hiring history - not just the "payment verified" badge. If they have 0 hires and the job looks too good to be true, skip it.

3. Build proof outside the platform.
High-ticket clients Google your name before they hire you. Your off-platform presence is now your competitive advantage.

The uncomfortable truth:
Upwork isn't broken. It's changing. And the freelancers who adapt first are the ones who win.

What's your experience been like on Upwork in 2026?
Still applying to everything? Shifted to a positioning-first strategy? Or figuring it out as you go?

Drop a comment. I'll reply to every single one.

One thing I've started paying more attention to is whether a decision is reversible.
Some decisions are difficult to undo.
Others aren't.
Hiring a new executive is different from testing a new workflow for two weeks.
Building an entire AI infrastructure is different from running a small pilot.
Signing a long-term contract is different from trying a new supplier on a limited basis.
Yet organizations sometimes treat all decisions as if they require the same level of commitment.
They don't.
For reversible decisions, speed and learning can matter more.
For irreversible decisions, slowing down can be valuable.
This sounds simple.
But it changes the question a leader asks.
Instead of:
“How confident are we?”
sometimes ask:
“How costly would it be to change our mind?”
If changing your mind is cheap, you may not need perfect information.
If changing your mind is expensive, you probably need much more thought before committing.
Good strategy isn't about avoiding uncertainty.
It's about understanding the cost of being wrong.

The most dangerous assumption in supply chain strategy for 2026 is that resilience comes from holding more inventory. It does not. It comes from having a data fabric that can reallocate inventory across modes, geographies, and priorities in minutes, not weeks.

I have spent the last year working directly with teams trying to operationalize the shift toward multimodal supply chains as a standard operating model. The non-obvious lesson is that the bottleneck is rarely the physical logistics. It is the contract and compliance layer. When you move from ocean to air or from rail to autonomous last-mile delivery, the cost structure, the regulatory documents, and the liability terms all change. Without a digital negotiation layer that can instantly evaluate these trade-offs, the team defaults to the slowest, most expensive option out of fear of a compliance violation.

Another trend reshaping the field is the integration of cybersecurity into the supply chain data pipeline. In 2025, the most disruptive attacks were not on the warehouse management system itself, but on the sensor data feeding the predictive maintenance models. If your inventory optimization algorithm is relying on data from a compromised sensor, your "optimal" reorder point is actually a liability. The teams that are pulling ahead are embedding anomaly detection directly into the data ingestion layer, not just at the network perimeter.

The human-machine collaboration piece is also more nuanced than most believe. I have seen planners successfully delegate routine exception handling to AI agents, but only when the agent is trained on the specific trade-off preferences of that planner, not a generic company policy. When the agent can explain why it chose to expedite one shipment over another using the planner's own historical reasoning, trust accelerates rapidly.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the person who can run a standard ERP module or build a single forecast model. You need someone who can design the contract-aware data pipelines that make multimodal switching viable, who understands how to model cybersecurity risk as a supply chain variable, and who can build the feedback loops that align AI agents with human decision-making. I am actively exploring the next challenge where I can apply these systems-thinking principles to build a supply chain that is resilient, not just efficient.

What is the one data-quality signal you monitor that tells you your supply chain is truly ready for a multimodal switch, not just theoretically capable?

I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.
 
"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"
 
I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
 
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.
 
That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:

Send request → check status code → check response body

What seniors answer:

Contract validation across consumers
Schema drift detection
State injection to remove UI dependency
Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail
 
The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
 
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.
 
It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.
 
What was your "I didn't know what I didn't know" API testing moment?
